🟠 AI expertise isn’t the same as AI oversight. Boards need both

Before we figure out what competent oversight involves, we need to be clear about what directors are meant to be overseeing. 

The following areas, drawn from our ongoing research [https://lnkd.in/gp3v69K5] into how directors oversee AI, are foundational. 

Each of these is a place where AI can do real damage to a company, and a board that covers some of them but not the others is dangerously exposed.

→ Governance Oversight: Knowing which individual is accountable for each AI matter, and making sure that they are actually held accountable.

→ Data Inquiry: Knowing what data the company’s AI uses, where it goes, and on what legal basis. This must be backed by evidence rather than a vendor’s assurance.

→ Explanation & Disclosure: Making sure the company can explain an AI decision to the person it was made about, and that its public claims about AI match what it does.

→ Fairness & Affected Parties: Knowing which groups a system could disadvantage, when it was last tested, and whether problems were fixed rather than just recorded.

→ Risk & Irreversibility: Knowing what the company’s AI can do that cannot be undone, and how the board would hear about a failure.

→ Human Judgment & Workforce: Making sure a person can overrule a system in practice, not just on paper, and that the people whose work AI changes are part of the plan.

→ Autonomy & Agent Authority: Knowing what AI agents may do, spend, and commit on their own, and making sure each one has a limit and a way to stop it.

That is what a board needs to oversee. But how do you actually build competent oversight of those areas? 

Three principles help you get there.
